titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §89–100: The erased columns II — merchants and loans (from the Nippur tablet)
part: Laws §89–100 · The erased columns II (the Nippur tablet)
about: The stele is erased here. After §65 the last seven columns of the front of the stone (XVII–XXIII, in Ungnad’s count) were chiselled smooth in antiquity, probably when the Elamite conquerors carried the stele away to Susa, and the laws that stood there reach us only from other ancient copies of the code. This second part of the erased section comes from a single copy: the Nippur tablet, an Old Babylonian school copy of the code, found at Nippur, now in the University Museum in Philadelphia (PBS V no. 93), whose reverse has six columns of some sixty lines each, the laws separated by ruled lines. It is broken: large stretches are lost at the head and foot of its columns, and each lost stretch is shown below as a gap […], never filled in. What survives is the merchant-and-loan block: the tail of a law before §90, the rate of interest (§90: for grain and for silver), the debtor with no silver who pays in grain by the king’s schedule and the creditor who demands more and loses what he lent (§91), more broken laws on interest, the end of a law on a creditor’s accounts, in which a creditor who adds interest to the capital pays back double (§94, partly guesswork), the creditor who lends by a small measure (§95), a loan made on a day marked by signs not understood (§96), the borrower who pays in goods before witnesses (§97), a lost law ending in the death penalty (§98), the partnership law (§99) and the opening of the agent law (§100), whose end is on the stele at §100–101. The numbers 89–100 are Ungnad’s approximate ones, adjusted so that none is used twice with the stele; Cuq’s numbering of the same tablet differs. The signs follow Cuq’s 1918 printing of Scheil’s reading of the tablet, and Poebel’s autograph (Plate XL) is a mosaic of small fragments that I looked at but could not read sign by sign: the check of every line against the plate was not completed, the notes say where a doubt remains, and the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs. The Assyrian copy DT 81 has a parallel to §97, mentioned in that law’s note but not drafted.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. I lines 1–3 (the last words of a law before §90; about 30 lines above are broken away)
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. This is only the tail of a law whose beginning is broken away, with about thirty lines above it, so its subject cannot be told. Three scraps of lines survive, a few signs each: …tu-šu, …te-šu and …ru-šum. The grammar gives only the ending -šum on the last line, “to him”, after a verb whose stem is lost (the editors restore “they shall give back”, [u-ta-ar]-ru-šum, but that is not adopted). The editor marks tu and te as doubtful; in the printing, [i-t]e(?), the bracket falls inside the sign TE, so it is read as a partly preserved TE, as with the other syllables split by a bracket in this part. The number 89 is Ungnad’s approximate one, chosen to fit the Nippur laws into the numbering; the real position is unknown. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. I lines 5–12 (loans at interest: the rate)
sentences.l: If merchant-[…] silver, for-the-loan [he-gave]: for 1 GUR.É […] of-grain interest he-shall-take. If silver for-the-loan [he-ga]ve: for 1 shekel of-silver one-sixth (and) 6 grain, interest, he-shall-take.
sentences.i: If a merchant has given […] silver as a loan, he shall take as interest, for each 1 GUR.É, […] of grain. If he has given silver as a loan, he shall take as interest, for 1 shekel of silver, one-sixth (of a shekel) and 6 grains.
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. The law fixes the rate of interest on a loan, the first of the merchant-and-loan laws on this tablet. It is the šumma-protasis of the stele’s laws (“If …”) followed by the rule. The loan is written ana ḪAR.RA, a Sumerogram which the next laws show to mean the loan, ḫubullum (§95 spells ḫu-bu-ul-li-im and then has ḪAR.RA again for the same thing); that value is from context, not confirmed. The measure is written 1 GUR.É (the editors print GUR-É): GUR is the large grain-measure, but I cannot say what the É adds, and the amount after it (editors’ [60+40(qa)], 100 qa) is their restoration, not adopted. The rate on silver is written IGI 6 GAL 6 ŠE: one-sixth (of a shekel) and 6 še, the small grain-weight; at 180 še to the shekel that is 36 še, a fifth of the shekel. The grain in the first half is itself lost ([še’am] after dam-); it is implied by the grain amount in line 3 and by the “grain, silver” of the next laws. ileqqi is “he shall take” (leqûm); iddin “he gave”. Where the editors print a plain Akkadian word (kaspam, še’am, ṣibtam, šiqil) the tablet’s own signs are a logogram, and I write it as in the stele’s laws and §66: KÙ.BABBAR, ŠE-am, MÁŠ, GÍN; where they print a spelled-out vowel (kaspa-am, kaspi-im, še-e-im) I kept every printed sign after the logogram. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. I lines 14–27 (the debtor with no silver pays in grain by the king's schedule; the creditor who demands more loses all)
sentences.l: If a-man who a-loan [he-]took, silver for-repaying not has, grain-only has, according-to the-schedule of-the-king, [the-merchant] for his-interest 1 […] of-grain-only he-shall-take; if the-merchant ik(?)-[…], interest 1 GUR.É […] […] interest he-increases-and, he-took(?), from anything that he-gave he-[forfeits].
sentences.i: If a man who has taken a loan has no silver to repay it but has only grain, then, according to the king’s schedule, [the merchant] shall take, for his interest, 1 […] of grain only. But if the merchant [refuses (?)] and the interest, 1 GUR.É […] […] the interest, he increases the interest and has taken (it) (?), he forfeits whatever he gave.
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. A debtor who owes silver but has only grain pays in grain at the king’s rate; a creditor who exceeds the rate loses what he lent. What you need to read it: ša ḫubullam [ilqû] “who took a loan” (the stele’s ša … ilqû relative clause); kaspam ana turrim lā īšu, “has not silver to repay” (turrim is the D-stem infinitive of târum, “to give back”); ŠE-a-am-ma, “grain only”, with the -ma that restricts (as in the stele’s clause chains); kīma ṣimdat šarrim, “according to the king’s schedule” (the ṣimdat šarrim of §§42–51, a fixed royal rate). The editors’ restored words fill the lost stretches of lines 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 14, but I do not adopt them, so the second half is only partly readable: of ik(?)-[kir-ma] only ik survives (and the editor doubts it); the rest is the editors’ restoration, so “refuses (?)” (nakārum, “to deny, dispute”) is only a guess at the verb, u₂-wa-at-te-[ir-ma] as uwattir-ma, “he increases (it) and”, from watārum, “to be surplus”. il-qi₂ is read ilqi, “he took”; the “i[l]” of line 13 is a damaged sign. The law ends with the stele’s forfeit formula, ina mimma ša iddinu ītelli, “he forfeits whatever he gave”. Lines 9–11 are mostly lost; if the editors’ restorations are right they repeat the rates of §90, but the signs there are not adopted and the English leaves them as gaps. Where the editors print a plain Akkadian word (kaspam, še’am, ṣibtam, šiqil) the tablet’s own signs are a logogram, and I write it as in the stele’s laws and §66: KÙ.BABBAR, ŠE-am, MÁŠ, GÍN; where they print a spelled-out vowel (kaspa-am, kaspi-im, še-e-im) I kept every printed sign after the logogram. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. I lines 29–35 (a creditor who has taken the interest … ; the end of the law, about five lines, is broken away)
sentences.l: If a-merchant grain […] for-interest [he-gave-]and interest ma […] of-grain (of)-silver […] he-took-and […] mi […] grain and silver [interest]-its not [is-there].
sentences.i: If a merchant [has given] grain […] at interest, and […] interest […] of grain (and) silver […] he has taken, and […] — the grain and the silver, its [interest] does not [exist].
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. A broken law about a merchant who gave grain and silver at interest and then took something (il-te-qi₂-ma, “he has taken”, from leqûm in the perfect with -ma); the middle of each line is lost (the editor’s dots stand for signs that cannot be read), so the condition cannot be read through, and I cannot say what was taken or why. What survives clearly is the end: še-um u kaspu-um … ṣibat-zu a-ul ib-ba-ši, “the grain and the silver — its interest does not exist”: the case endings -um show the two are the subject of the sentence, and the last words, ul … ši, are probably “there is not” (bašûm; the verb itself, [ib-ba]-ši, is the editors’ restoration). The first sign of ṣibat-zu is lost, and zu is the suffix -šu, “its”, spelled with z after a t (compare MÁŠ-zu, ṣibassu, in gap-a §66); the established line has za, but Cuq’s page prints [ṣibat]zu, so I read zu (not checked on the plate); no interest is owed. The five lines that closed the law are lost and are shown below as a gap. The editors’ restored [id-di-in-m]a and [ib-ba]-ši are not adopted; the mi in line 5 stands alone between gaps. Where the editors print a plain Akkadian word (kaspam, še’am, ṣibtam, šiqil) the tablet’s own signs are a logogram, and I write it as in the stele’s laws and §66: KÙ.BABBAR, ŠE-am, MÁŠ, GÍN; where they print a spelled-out vowel (kaspa-am, kaspi-im, še-e-im) I kept every printed sign after the logogram. sentences.ref: Nippur col. I, five lines lost at the foot of the column (Cuq: 'Manquent 5 lignes')
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. Five lines of the Nippur tablet are broken away at the foot of column I; nothing of them survives in any edition, and they are shown as a gap, not filled in. They would have carried the end of this law and perhaps the start of the next. sentences.ref: Nippur col. II, about twenty lines lost at the head of the column — all of Cuq's article 93 and the beginning of article 94
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. About twenty lines are lost at the head of column II of the Nippur tablet: all of Cuq’s article 93 and the beginning of his article 94. The numbers are Ungnad’s approximate ones for the Nippur laws (§93 stands here only for the lost law), and nothing of the text is known; this is a gap, not a reconstruction. sentences.ref: Nippur col. II lines 1–8 (the end of the law: a creditor who has not entered the repayment or written a supplementary tablet, or who adds interest to capital, pays back double what he took)
sentences.l: Or grain […]; as-much-as il(?)[…]; not he-had-dug(?)[-it]-and, an-upper tablet not he-wrote, or interest to the-head he-added: that merchant, grain-only that not he-took, he-shall-double-and he-shall-return.
sentences.i: Or grain […]; as much as [he took (?)] […]; and he has not had (it) scratched out (?) […], and has not written a supplementary (?) tablet, or has added interest to the capital — that merchant shall double the grain which he did not take (?), and give it back.
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. The end of a law about a creditor’s accounts (its beginning is in the twenty lines lost at the head of this column). What you need to read it: u-lu is ulu, “or”; mala il…, “as much as …” (only il survives, a damaged sign the editor doubts; “he took” is the editors’ restoration [il-qu₂-u₂], not adopted); lā … iš-ṭu-ur, “he did not write”; dup-pa-am e-li-am is literally “an upper tablet” (eliûm, “upper, higher”); “supplementary” is the editors’ understanding of it, which I keep with a question mark; ṣibātim ana qaqqadim uttēḫḫi, “he added the interest to the head” (SAG.DU, qaqqadum, is the capital sum): that is, compound interest. The verb uš-ta-aḫ-ri-[šu]-ma of line 3 is doubtful both as a reading (the editor flags it) and as a word; I took it as a Š-stem of ḫerûm, whose plain meaning is “to dig” (also “to scratch”); “he had it scratched out (?)”, that is, struck from the debt tablet, is only a guess from the sense of the whole sentence, not something the grammar gives. The penalty is in lines 7–8: uštašannâ-ma utâr, “he shall double (it) and give it back” (utâr is the D-stem durative of târum). What he doubles is written še-amma lā ilqû, “the grain that he did not take”: the grammar is clear, but the sense is not, and the editors’ summary (the double of what he took) may be what the lost words in line 1 meant. The restored words after še- in line 1 and after il- in line 2 are not adopted. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. II lines 10–21 (a creditor who gave with a small measure and took with a large one loses all; lines 13 and 17–18 are very doubtful)
sentences.l: If a-merchant grain and silver for-a-loan he-gave-and, when for-the-loan he-gave, silver […] ni-im small(?) and grain by-the-GIŠ.BAR small he-gave, and when he-received, silver(?) […] ni(?) im […], grain […], he-received […] from anything […] he-for[feits].
sentences.i: If a merchant has given grain and silver as a loan, and when he gave (it) as a loan he gave the silver […] small (?) […], and gave the grain by a small GIŠ.BAR measure, and when he received (it) […] silver (?) […] grain […] he received […] he forfeits [whatever he gave].
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. A merchant who lends by a small measure and (it seems) takes back by a large one loses the loan; the second half of the law is lost. The law is only half readable: lines 4 and 8–9 of it (the tablet’s lines 13 and 17–18) are very doubtful, and the matching phrases are lost. What you need to read it: ana ḫubullim iddin-ma, “he gave as a loan, and”, then inūma ana ḪAR.RA iddinu, “when he gave as a loan (ḪAR.RA again)”; the measure is ina GIŠ-BAR maṭītim, “by a small GIŠ.BAR measure” — GIŠ.BAR is a Sumerogram that evidently names a measure, and I did not establish its Akkadian reading; maṭītim is the feminine “small, short” (maṭûm), with ma and ṭi both marked doubtful by the editor; the lost matching phrase (the large measure, taken at the repayment, after u inūma imḫuru, “and when he received”) I cannot supply. The ending, imḫur dam-qar šū … ina mimma ša iddinu ītelli, is the code’s forfeit formula (“that merchant forfeits whatever he gave”), whose first words and last words are broken, so it is shown with gaps. In our line 8 (tablet line 17) the editor doubts both kaspa-am and ni, and our line 9 (tablet line 18) is only še; our line 4 is tablet line 13. Where the editors print a plain Akkadian word (kaspam, še’am, ṣibtam, šiqil) the tablet’s own signs are a logogram, and I write it as in the stele’s laws and §66: KÙ.BABBAR, ŠE-am, MÁŠ, GÍN; where they print a spelled-out vowel (kaspa-am, kaspi-im, še-e-im) I kept every printed sign after the logogram. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. II lines 23–28 (a loan made on a day when the control (NER) did not … loses all; Cuq notes that three clearly visible signs, ûm NER la, were left untranscribed by Scheil)
sentences.l: If a-merchant […] for-ḫu[…] […], day NER not […] he-gave, from anything [that he-]gave he-forfeits.
sentences.i: If a merchant […] [as a loan] […], (on) a day (when?) NER (did) not […] he gave (it), he forfeits whatever he gave.
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. A merchant who made a loan, apparently under a condition now lost, forfeits whatever he gave; what the condition was is not readable. Line 3 shows three clearly visible signs, UD (ūm, “day”), NER and la (lā, “not”), which Cuq says Scheil left untranscribed; the editors’ ûm NER la is their reading, and I wrote the three signs as printed, with NER as the KIŠ sign read ner (Harper’s sign list gives ner for it). What NER means here is not clear: the editors’ own note calls it a “control”, and I do not know the word, so it has no gloss beyond that; the sense “on a day when … not …” is a guess from the three signs. The rest is the forfeit formula, ina mimma ša iddinu ītelli, “he forfeits whatever he gave”, broken in lines 5–6; the opening of the law and the middle are shown as gaps. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. II lines 30–40 (the borrower with no silver or grain delivers his goods before witnesses and the creditor must accept; Cuq's line 36 reads ga-ti-šu = qa-ti-šu; the same law is on the Assyrian tablet DT 81 col. IV, which Ungnad numbers 'cca. 96' — see parallels)
sentences.l: If a-man grain and silver with a-merchant he-took-and, grain and silver for repaying not he-has, [goods]-am-ma he-has: anything in his-hand that is-there, before witnesses as he-brings, to his-merchant he-shall-give; the-merchant not u-pa-aṣ (?), he-shall-receive.
sentences.i: If a man has taken grain and silver from a merchant, and has no grain or silver to repay it, but he has [goods]: whatever is in his hand, he shall give to his merchant before witnesses, as he brings (it). The merchant shall not u-pa-aṣ (a verb I cannot read); he shall receive (it).
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. A borrower with no grain or silver to repay with, but with goods, hands over whatever he has before witnesses, and the creditor must take it. What you need to read it: the šumma-clause with the -ma clause chain (il-qi₂-e-ma … , “he took, and”); the words ana turrim lā īšû, “not has for repaying” as in §91; mimma ina qātīšu ibaššû, “whatever there is in his hand” (qātum, “hand”: the sign GA is read qa, so qa-ti-šu; the editors print ga-ti-šu, which Cuq says is qa-ti-šu, and the editor marks the reading doubtful); maḫar šībī kīma ubbalu, “before witnesses as he brings (it)”, with kīma and the subjunctive ubbalu (wabālum, “to carry”). The last line is hard: dam-qar u-ul u-pa-aṣ i-ma-ḫar, “the merchant … not …, he shall receive”; u-pa-aṣ is doubtful (the Assyrian copy has up-pa-aš-ma, which may be the same word spelled differently, but that is not certain), and I could not establish its verb from the grammar: it is left as written, upaṣ, and not translated. That the merchant must accept the goods is the sense of the whole law; the verb before imaḫḫar is not understood. Cuq’s page prints the last word as i-ma ḫa-ar (two signs, ḫa and ar); the established line, which I follow, has one sign ḫar — not checked on the plate. The same law is in the Assyrian copy DT 81, col. IV (Kuyunjik; Ungnad numbers it “cca. 96”, so the numbers there and here differ): its text is not drafted here, only noted; the Assyrian text has small variants (ša for ina, tamkarum šū, ul uppaš-ma imaḫḫar) and is entirely italic, that is restored from this Assyrian text, in the editors’ print. The word before the gap in line 6 is restored by the editors as [bi-ša]-am-ma, “goods”; only the end, am-ma, survives, and the following i-šu is, as printed, “he has”. Where the editors print a plain Akkadian word (kaspam, še’am, ṣibtam, šiqil) the tablet’s own signs are a logogram, and I write it as in the stele’s laws and §66: KÙ.BABBAR, ŠE-am, MÁŠ, GÍN; where they print a spelled-out vowel (kaspa-am, kaspi-im, še-e-im) I kept every printed sign after the logogram. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. III line 1 (the penalty at the end of a lost law: 'he shall be killed')
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. One word, the penalty at the end of a law whose beginning is lost: id-da-ak, iddâk, “he shall be killed” (the code’s usual wording for the death penalty: the N-stem, passive, of dâkum, “to kill”). Nothing of the offence survives, so I cannot say who is killed or why; the law before it is the gap above. The number 98 is Ungnad’s approximate one. sentences.ref: Nippur col. III lines 3–7 (partners: profit and loss are shared equally before the gods; Cuq's 'article 100')
sentences.l: If a-man to a-man silver for-partnership he-gave, profit and loss that arise before the-gods equally they-shall-divide.
sentences.i: If a man has given silver to another man for a partnership, they shall divide equally, before the gods, whatever profit and loss arise.
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. A man who invests silver with another in a partnership: profit and loss are shared equally, before the gods (perhaps meaning under oath). This is the law that Cuq numbers “article 100”; here it is §99 so that no number is used twice with the stele (the next law, §100, is the beginning of the agent law whose end is on the stele at §100–101). What you need to read it: šumma awīlum ana awīlim, “if a man (gives) to a man”; ana tappûtim, “for a partnership” (tappûtum, “partnership”; the editors print it as one normalized word, so TAB-BU-TIM, as in the established line, is a syllabic placeholder and not certainly the tablet’s signs); nemēlam u butuqqâm, “profit and loss” (nemēlum, “gain”; butuqqûm, “loss, a claim of loss”); the relative ša ibbašû, “which arise” (the N-stem of bašûm, “to be there, come to be”, as in §66); maḫar ilāni, “before the gods”, where the editors print ilāni, a plural logogram; I write it DINGIR.DINGIR, as the stele does, since the tablet’s own signs are not recorded; and mitḫāriš izuzzu, “they shall divide equally”: izuzzū is the present, 3rd plural, of zâzum, “to divide”, and mitḫāriš, “equally”, is an adverb. This is the best-preserved law of this part, but the sign-by-sign check against the plate was not completed. Where the editors print a plain Akkadian word (kaspam, še’am, ṣibtam, šiqil) the tablet’s own signs are a logogram, and I write it as in the stele’s laws and §66: KÙ.BABBAR, ŠE-am, MÁŠ, GÍN; where they print a spelled-out vowel (kaspa-am, kaspi-im, še-e-im) I kept every printed sign after the logogram. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.

sentences.ref: Nippur col. III lines 9–19 (the merchant gives silver to his agent to trade; the agent goes on a journey; the opening of the law whose last lines are the stele's §100–101. Cuq restores lines 16–19 from the Louvre text, which this firing does not adopt as signs; lines 20–29 are on the stele and are not repeated here)
sentences.l: If the-merchant to the-agent silver for [selling(?)] [and] [receiving(?)] he-gave-and, on-a-journey he-sent-him; the-agent on-the-journey […]-to-him […] uṣṣap(?) […] [where] he-went […] he-saw.
sentences.i: If a merchant has given silver to an agent for […] and […] and has sent him on a journey, the agent on the journey […] to him […] he adds (?) […] [where] he went […] he has seen […].
sentences.n: From the Nippur tablet (siglum Nippur), an Old Babylonian school copy of the code found at Nippur (University Museum, Philadelphia, PBS V no. 93, reverse, Plate XL); the stele itself is erased here. The opening of the agent law, the last part of which stands on the stele at §100–101: a merchant gives silver to his agent to trade with and sends him on a journey. The number 100 is Ungnad’s approximate one; the law continues on the stele at §100–101 (lines 20–29 of the Nippur column are those, and are not repeated here), and the Ungnad and Cuq numbers are only approximate and differ. What you need to read it: šamallûm is the merchant’s agent (Cuq prints šamalli-im and šamallû, a logogram with a complement, so the tablet’s signs are not the syllables I used; I wrote it with syllables, which is a placeholder and not the tablet’s signs); ana pašārim [u maḫārim], “for selling [and receiving]” is the editors’ restoration (not adopted); only pa-ša… and …ḫa-ri… of it survive, the sa of pa-š[a-rim] and the ḫa of [ma-ḫ]a-ri-[im] being damaged signs, and the sense is partly guessed; id-di-in-ma, “he gave, and”; ana ḫarrānim iṭrussu, “he sent him on a journey” (Cuq prints ḫarranim as one unhyphenated word, as he prints logograms, so the tablet may write it with the sign KASKAL; the established text and this unit give the syllabic ḫar-ra-nim, not checked on the plate): iṭrussu is iṭrud, the preterite of ṭarādum, “to send”, plus -šu, “him”, the d assimilating to the š (-ssu); it is written it-ru-uz-zu; šamallû ina ḫarrānim, “the agent, on the journey”. The three lines after it are heavily broken: [… ki]-du-šum, “…-to-him”; […] uṣ-ṣa-ap(?), a form I cannot place (the editor doubts the last sign), which I took, with doubt, as uṣṣap from eṣēpum, “to add”; and (ašar) illiku, ītamar, “(where) he went”, “he has seen”, the first words of a clause “where he went, he has seen (profit)”, which the editors restore with [ne-me-lam], “profit”, not adopted. Cuq restores lines 16–19 from the Louvre text; that is not adopted as signs. Where the editors print a plain Akkadian word (kaspam, še’am, ṣibtam, šiqil) the tablet’s own signs are a logogram, and I write it as in the stele’s laws and §66: KÙ.BABBAR, ŠE-am, MÁŠ, GÍN; where they print a spelled-out vowel (kaspa-am, kaspi-im, še-e-im) I kept every printed sign after the logogram. Broken or doubtful signs (marked (?) by the editors, or damaged) are uncertain; the editors’ restorations in [ ] are not adopted as signs and show here as gaps. The signs follow Cuq’s printed reading (Scheil’s) with the standard Old Babylonian sign for each syllable; I did not complete a sign-by-sign check against Poebel’s Plate XL, which is a mosaic of small fragments.
